newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Communists to join Jospin government.
newsitem.headline: French Communists to join Jospin government.

text.p: The French Communist Party said on Wednesday it would join the Socialist-led government of new Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, the first time it has helped rule since 1984.

Party boss Robert Hue said he would not take a ministerial portfolio in the new government so he could devote his energy to running the party. The Communists won the balance of power in Sunday's National Assembly election won by the Socialists.

"After democratic consultation of party members, the national committee of the French Communist Party has decided on the participation of Communist ministers in the French government," Hue told a news conference.
The decision confirms a recommendation by party leaders on Tuesday.

The Communists, who oppose a single European Union currency and want wage increases for the lowest-paid, said the Socialists had "satisfactorily" taken Communist views into account in defining the new government's policies.

Jospin aides have said the Communists may get two ministries and one post of secretary of state in the new left-wing government. A senior aide to Jospin said the new government would be named later on Wednesday.

It will be the first time in 13 years that the Communists have held cabinet posts. After serving under late president Francois Mitterrand from 1981-1984 the Communists left the government, accusing him of betraying the Socialist ideal.

The Communists held the balance of power in the parliament when a Socialist-led government ruled from 1988 to 1993, but did not participate in policy-making. The end of the Cold War further disoriented the once Stalinist party.

The Socialists and Communists signed a pre-election declaration in April outlining plans to cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 without loss of pay and to create 700,000 youth jobs. But the Communists want both measures implemented far faster than the Socialists.
The Communist party won 38 of 577 National Assembly seats in Sunday's parliamentary election. The non-Communist left won 274 seats -- short of the 289 needed for a majority.

Hue remained silent on Wednesday on what if any conditions he posed as the price for joining Jospin's government, saying only that the Party wanted clear signs the Socialists would carry through pledges of change.

Jospin repeatedly said during the campaign that leftists wanting to take part in a Socialist-led government would have to bow to the Socialist line. Unlike the Communists, the Socialists broadly favour the euro single currency.

Hue spoke to Jospin on Tuesday and reiterated demands for an immediate increase in the minimum monthly wage, a two percentage point cut in general value added tax and bigger cuts in VAT on basic products.
